Used to catch the invasive Sacramento Perch in Lake Crawley near Bishop California by the bucketful. Haven't fished there since 2008, but it got hard to catch that fish because it tasted good and everyone was encouraged to fish for it.
I don't understand the idea that no ecosystem should ever change.

" In areas the fish has invaded, the biomass of native reef fish species has dropped by an average of 65 percent." The article also supplied the link to the scientific study in question. So, in this particular case, it is more about the ecosystem shrinking like Detroit than just a change.
That's how ecosystems change. An "invasive species" comes in and everything else has to adapt. We can't lock down the whole world and we shouldn't try.

Massive decreases in biodiversity caused by a single invasive species cause all sorts of problems. The life in the environment becomes less resistant to things like fire, famine, drought, and other invasive species that basically just pass through and eat/kill everything that they like. If the only thing they like is the only thing that's there, then when they're done, there's nothing left. You have a desert.

Obviously ecosystems are going to change and evolve but that process is typically gradual. Plants and animals didn't just get instantly injected into new areas like they do now. The existing plants and animals had time to adapt.
